In parallel, C. albicans colonization enhanced adipose mitochondrial respiration and thermogenic programming while promoting a Type 17 immune response, revealing coordinated metabolic and immune adaptations. Genetic deficiency of γδ T cells partially reversed the metabolic phenotype, demonstrating that this immune function contributes to fungal regulation of host energy balance. Together, our findings demonstrate that coordinated interactions among the microbiota, microbial metabolites and the immune system constrain host energy storage by simultaneously limiting nutrient acquisition and enhancing energy expenditure. More broadly, these findings establish intestinal fungi as potent regulators of host metabolism and reveal that low-abundance members of the microbiome can exert disproportionate physiological effects through interkingdom ecological interactions.
ids: title:gut commensal candida albicans constrains whole body energy storage in mice

title: Mechanistic study of cycloastragenol in improving heart failure by regulating PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling and ferroptosis.
abstract: Heart failure (HF) is the end stage of various cardiovascular diseases, and persistent myocardial injury and adverse remodeling are major causes of its high hospitalization and mortality rates worldwide. Therefore, it is important to identify key molecules and effective agents that can slow or reverse HF progression. Cycloastragenol (CAG) is an active compound derived from Astragalus and has anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and tissue-protective effects. The present study aimed to clarify the protective role of CAG in HF and to determine whether this effect is related to the regulation of ferroptosis through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway. The results showed that PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling activity was markedly decreased in myocardial tissue from HF rats, accompanied by impaired cardiac function, aggravated myocardial injury, enhanced inflammatory response, and increased myocardial fibrosis and hypertrophic remodeling. At the same time, GSH levels were decreased, whereas ROS, MDA, and Fe2+ levels were increased. In addition, GPX4 and FTH1 expression was downregulated, ACSL4 expression was upregulated, and the Prussian blue-positive area was increased, indicating marked ferroptosis-related abnormalities. After CAG treatment, these changes were improved to different degrees. CAG restored cardiac function, reduced serum NT-proBNP, CK-MB, and cTnI levels, decreased inflammatory factor expression, and alleviated myocardial fibrosis and hypertrophy. Meanwhile, PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling activity was restored, and iron deposition, lipid peroxidation, and ferroptosis-related molecular abnormalities were alleviated. In vitro experiments further showed that, in an OGD-induced H9c2 cell injury model, CAG increased cell viability, reduced LDH release, attenuated the inflammatory response, and alleviated mitochondrial membrane potential loss, ROS accumulation, and ferroptosis-related protein abnormalities. C11-BODIPY 581/591 flow cytometry further demonstrated that CAG reduced OGD-induced lipid ROS accumulation and lipid peroxidation. In addition, the ferroptosis inhibitor ferrostatin-1 partially rescued OGD-induced cell injury, restored cell viability, reduced LDH release, and suppressed lipid ROS accumulation, further supporting the involvement of ferroptosis-related processes. Further intervention with the AKT inhibitor MK-2206 partially weakened the protective effects of CAG, supporting the involvement of AKT signaling in its protective action. In conclusion, the present study showed that CAG improved HF-related myocardial injury and myocardial remodeling by restoring PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling activity and inhibiting ferroptosis-related processes, suggesting that CAG may be a potential therapeutic agent for HF.
ids: title:mechanistic study of cycloastragenol in improving heart failure by regulating pi3k akt mtor signaling and ferroptosis

title: Preoperative Magnetic Resonance Imaging-Derived Adiposity Profiling and Cardiometabolic Remodeling After Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery.
abstract: Cardiometabolic remodeling after metabolic and bariatric surgery is heterogeneous and may not be fully characterized by clinical measures. This exploratory pilot study examined whether abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived adiposity profiles, combined with clinical and echocardiographic data, could identify preoperative patterns associated with 12-month cardiometabolic remodeling after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG). This prospective study included 40 adults with severe obesity who underwent LSG. Baseline clinical characteristics, MRI-derived subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT), visceral adipose tissue, liver fat fraction, and transthoracic echocardiographic parameters were evaluated in relation to 12-month changes in body weight (BW), glycated hemoglobin (A1C), mean blood pressure (mean BP), and left ventricular mass index (LVMI). Elastic net regression with 1,000 bootstrap resamples was used to identify stable exploratory signals. At 12 months, participants achieved a BMI reduction of 14.78 ± 4.52 kg/m², corresponding to 90.01 ± 24.06% excess BMI loss, with significant improvements in A1C, mean BP, and LVMI (all p < 0.001). Higher baseline BW and A1C were associated with greater weight loss and glycemic improvement, respectively. Cardiovascular remodeling showed distinct patterns: higher baseline BP and greater abdominal SAT were associated with greater BP reduction, whereas greater baseline LVMI and lower estimated filling pressure were associated with more favorable cardiac reverse remodeling. Removing MRI variables reduced model performance for mean BP reduction and LVMI regression but had little effect on weight loss or glycemic improvement. MRI-derived adiposity measures may add selective information for cardiovascular remodeling after LSG, but require validation in larger independent cohorts.
ids: title:preoperative magnetic resonance imaging derived adiposity profiling and cardiometabolic remodeling after metabolic and bariatric surgery

title: Lysine Lactylation Modifies Cryab-Hspa1b Interactions and Prevents MAPK Signaling to Slow Diabetic Cardiomyopathy Progression.
abstract: Protein posttranslational modifications, including lactylation, have been intimately associated with myocardial energy metabolism. In this study, we investigated the role of Cryab in diabetic cardiomyopathy (DbCM) and its lysine lactylation (Kla). A spontaneous DbCM mouse model in db/db mice and a high-fat diet combined with i.p. streptozotocin injection mouse model were used. Primary cardiomyocytes were subjected to liposome-mediated transfection, followed by exposure to high glucose and palmitate. Cryab exhibited reduced Kla modification in myocardial tissue from DbCM mouse models and in damaged cardiomyocytes, while protein expression remained unchanged. Kla modification site mutation at K90R worsened cardiac systolic and diastolic dysfunction, myocardial hypertrophy, fibrosis, and apoptosis in vivo and in vitro. Cryab modulated the Hspa1b protein in a Kla-dependent manner and enhanced the stability of the Hspa1b protein. In DbCM mouse models or cardiomyocytes, Hspa1b protein expression was reduced, and the MAPK pathway was activated, which was further exacerbated following mutation at K90R. These findings demonstrate that reduced Kla modification in Cryab accelerated degradation of Hspa1b and activation of the MAPK pathway, thereby contributing to cardiac dysfunction associated with DbCM. These findings suggest that novel therapeutic strategies targeting protein Kla modification could be significant in the clinical management of DbCM. Cryab lysine lactylation (Kla) modification in myocardial tissue is reduced in db/db mice with diabetic cardiomyopathy (DbCM). Mutations in the Cryab Kla site exacerbate DbCM damage in vivo and in vitro. Cryab Kla enhances the stability of the Hspa1b protein by interacting with Hspa1b. Cryab blocks DbCM-induced MAPK signaling in an Hspa1b-dependent manner. Cryab/Hspa1b/MAPK signaling influences DbCM-associated cardiac dysfunction.
ids: title:lysine lactylation modifies cryab hspa1b interactions and prevents mapk signaling to slow diabetic cardiomyopathy progression

title: Identification and validation of brown adipocyte-related key genes in ST-segment elevated myocardial infarction.
abstract: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), a critical manifestation of coronary artery disease, involves complex molecular mechanisms potentially linked to brown adipocyte (BA) biology. This study aimed to identify BA-related key genes and elucidate their roles in STEMI progression. Transcriptomic data from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) of STEMI patients and stable coronary artery disease (CAD) controls were obtained from the GEO database (GSE59867, GSE62646). A 102-gene brown adipocyte-related gene (BARG) set was curated from published literature. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using limma, and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) combined with single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) was applied to detect BARG-associated module genes. The intersection of DEGs and module genes yielded 20 candidate genes, which were further refined using LASSO regression and SVM-RFE machine learning algorithms, identifying ASGR2, MCEMP1, and PPARG as key genes consistently upregulated in STEMI across both datasets. A nomogram model incorporating these three genes achieved an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.973, demonstrating excellent diagnostic performance. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed convergent enrichment of all three key genes in neutrophil degranulation and Toll-like receptor signaling cascades. Immune infiltration profiling using CIBERSORT identified significant increases in monocytes alongside decreases in resting NK cells and eosinophils in STEMI, with all three key genes showing significant correlations with these immune cell populations. Molecular docking identified shinpterocarpin as a candidate compound targeting PPARG with a suggestive binding affinity (-5.8 kcal/mol), warranting further experimental validation. RT-qPCR in an independent preliminary clinical cohort (n = 5 per group) demonstrated upregulation of all three key genes in STEMI patients (p < 0.05), consistent with bioinformatic predictions. This study identifies ASGR2, MCEMP1, and PPARG as BA-associated key genes in STEMI PBMC profiles and highlights their potential immune-metabolic relevance.
ids: title:identification and validation of brown adipocyte related key genes in st segment elevated myocardial infarction

title: Sex as a Biological Variable in Cardiovascular Pharmacology: A Practical Guide for Experimental Design
abstract: Sex is increasingly recognized as an important biological variable in cardiovascular research, yet its implications for experimental design and pharmacological interpretation are not always straightforward. Male and female experimental preparations may differ in baseline cardiovascular physiology, their response to disease-inducing stimuli, the progression of the resulting phenotype, and their response to pharmacological interventions. Consequently, applying the same experimental protocol to both sexes does not necessarily produce an equivalent biological challenge. This review provides a practical framework for integrating sex as a biological variable into experimental cardiovascular pharmacology, encompassing vascular function and blood pressure regulation, cardiac function and bioenergetics, ischemia–reperfusion injury, cardiac remodeling and heart failure, and electrophysiology. Particular emphasis is placed on studies in which males and females were investigated within the same experimental framework, allowing direct comparison under comparable conditions. Across experimental models, the direction and magnitude of sex differences vary with species, age, disease context, experimental duration, and endpoint. Importantly, an apparent sex difference in treatment response may reflect differences in the underlying model phenotype rather than genuinely sex-dependent pharmacological responsiveness. Recognizing these distinctions when selecting models, defining endpoints, and interpreting intervention studies should improve the rigor and translational relevance of cardiovascular pharmacology research involving both sexes.
ids: title:sex as a biological variable in cardiovascular pharmacology a practical guide for experimental design

title: Dimethylmalonate suppresses white adipocyte differentiation and ameliorates diet-induced obesity.
abstract: Obesity is driven by pathological expansion of white adipose tissue (WAT), reflecting both adipocyte hypertrophy and the differentiation of preadipocytes into mature white adipocytes. Arresting adipogenic differentiation is therefore a logical anti-obesity strategy. Because adipogenesis relies on extensive metabolic rewiring, blocking it by targeting mitochondrial enzymes-without collapsing cellular bioenergetics-remains an attractive but unresolved objective. Here, we investigated dimethylmalonate (DMM), a membrane-permeable diester that undergoes intracellular cleavage to yield malonate, a classic competitive inhibitor of succinate dehydrogenase (SDH). During the induced differentiation of 3T3-L1 preadipocytes, DMM treatment concentration-dependently restrained intracellular lipid accumulation. Furthermore, it markedly blunted the differentiation-induced induction of Pparg, which encodes the master transcriptional regulator of the white adipocyte lineage. Importantly, this occurred without bioenergetic collapse: viability remained near 90% at 10 mM, oxygen consumption was sustained and modestly increased, and intracellular ATP content rose. Concurrently, elevated cellular succinate confirmed robust on-target SDH inhibition. In a murine model of high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity, daily oral administration of DMM at 600 mg/kg, but not at 200 mg/kg, attenuated body weight gain and reduced both subcutaneous and visceral WAT mass. These morphological improvements were accompanied by improved glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity, with no significant alteration in daily food intake or in the mass of the liver, heart, and skeletal muscle. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that DMM suppresses white adipocyte differentiation and ameliorates diet-induced obesity while sustaining mitochondrial respiration and ATP content, highlighting targeted SDH modulation as a viable anti-obesity therapeutic strategy.
ids: title:dimethylmalonate suppresses white adipocyte differentiation and ameliorates diet induced obesity

title: Trends and Approaches in Obesity and Overweight Research Focused on White Adipose Tissue and Browning: A Bibliometric Study.
journal: Obesity reviews : an official journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity
abstract: The global rise in obesity has intensified scientific interest in adipose tissue biology, particularly the mechanisms underlying white adipose tissue (WAT) browning. This bibliometric study mapped the evolution, structure, and emerging directions of research on obesity, overweight, and WAT browning from 2011 to May 2025. Records were retrieved from Web of Science, Scopus, and PubMed and analyzed using VOSviewer, Bibliometrix, and Biblioshiny. A total of 2106 publications were identified, with a notable surge in output over the last decade. The United States, China, and several European countries emerged as leading contributors in terms of publication volume and citations. Influential journals were identified, highlighting interdisciplinary collaboration across molecular biology, endocrinology, and metabolic research. Keyword co-occurrence and trend-topic analyses identified thermogenesis, mitochondrial activity, transcriptional regulation, and adipocyte differentiation as central themes, whereas more recent research has shifted toward omics-based approaches, autophagy, gut microbiota, extracellular vesicles, immune regulation, and neuroendocrine pathways. Despite major mechanistic advances, the literature remains predominantly preclinical, and the contribution of beige adipocytes to whole-body energy expenditure in humans appears modest. Overall, the field has evolved from the identification of thermogenic adipocytes toward a more integrated view of adipose tissue plasticity and interorgan communication, although substantial challenges remain for clinical translation and long-term validation.
ids: title:trends and approaches in obesity and overweight research focused on white adipose tissue and browning a bibliometric study

title: Pharmacological inhibition of CLPP stabilizes LETMD1 to boost thermogenesis and alleviate obesity.
abstract: Obesity poses a severe global health burden, and activating adipose thermogenesis offers a promising therapeutic avenue. However, the contribution of mitochondrial proteostasis to thermogenic regulation remains elusive. Here, we identify mitochondrial protease CLPP as a negative regulator of adipose thermogenesis. Pharmacological suppression of CLPP activity enhances thermogenic programmes in adipocytes. Mechanistically, CLPP interacts with LETMD1 and promotes its degradation at the post-translational level, while LETMD1 stabilization is required for the thermogenic effects induced by CLPP suppression. In vivo , pharmacological suppression of CLPP activity using hinokiflavone significantly enhances energy expenditure, attenuates weight gain, and improves insulin sensitivity in obese mice. Collectively, our study identifies a CLPP-LETMD1 regulatory axis that regulates adipose thermogenesis and highlights CLPP suppression as a potential therapeutic strategy for obesity intervention.
ids: title:pharmacological inhibition of clpp stabilizes letmd1 to boost thermogenesis and alleviate obesity

title: The generation and characterization of CTRP9-CreERT2 knock-in mice for targeting endothelial cell muscle and adipose tissues.
abstract: Vascular endothelial cells (ECs) exhibit significant diversity in different tissues. To elucidate the distinct physiological roles of individual EC subtypes, genetic mouse lines utilizing the Cre-loxP recombination system are crucial. However, there is still a lack of Cre mouse lines that specifically target muscle ECs. Here, through analysis of publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing datasets, C1q/tumor necrosis factor-related protein-9 (CTRP9) was identified as a highly selective marker for microvascular ECs in muscle and adipose tissues. A CTRP9-CreERT2-tdTomato knock-in mouse line was then generated using CRISPR/Cas9, with tdTomato serving as a reporter for endogenous CTRP9 expression. By breeding these mice with Rosa26LSL-EYFP reporter mice and administering tamoxifen, specific EYFP and tdTomato expression was observed in CD31+ ECs in the heart, skeletal muscle, tongue, and adipose tissue from postnatal to adult stages. The EYFP+ cells were mainly identified as microvascular ECs, rather than arterial or venous ECs. The CTRP9-CreERT2 mouse model allows for precise and effective genetic manipulation of this distinct endothelial population, providing a valuable tool for investigating their roles in muscle metabolism, regeneration, and pathophysiology.
ids: title:the generation and characterization of ctrp9 creert2 knock in mice for targeting endothelial cell muscle and adipose tissues

title: Ganoderma lucidum polysaccharide protects against myocardial ischemic injury by restoring myocardial energy metabolism and alleviating oxidative stress in mice and AC16 cardiomyocytes.
abstract: Myocardial ischemic injury is characterized by impaired energy metabolism and oxidative stress, which contribute to cardiac dysfunction and disease progression. Ganoderma lucidum polysaccharide (GLP), a major bioactive component of Ganoderma lucidum, exhibits various pharmacological activities; however, its protective effects against myocardial ischemic injury and underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated the effects of GLP against isoproterenol (ISO)-induced myocardial ischemic injury and its involvement in metabolic regulation and oxidative stress. A mouse myocardial ischemic injury model was established by subcutaneous injection of ISO (2 mg/kg/day) for 11days. Mice were randomly divided into normal control, model, GLP treatment groups with GLP administered orally at 50 and 100 mg/kg/day, and at 50 mg/kg/day by intraperitoneal injection. An ISO-induced injury model in vitro was established using AC16 cardiomyocytes, which were pretreated with GLP (0.25 ~ 1.00 µg/mL) followed by ISO exposure (40 µM, 24 h). GLP significantly alleviated ISO-induced myocardial injury, reduced cardiac hypertrophy, improved histopathological alterations, and decreased serum AST and LDH activities in mice. Similar protective effects were observed in AC16 cells. Moreover, GLP restored myocardial energy metabolic homeostasis, by improving ATP, phosphocreatine, creatine, and total adenine nucleotides levels, while reducing cAMP accumulation. GLP also alleviated oxidative stress by decreasing malondialdehyde level and enhancing total superoxide dismutase activity. Furthermore, GLP increased the expression of AMPK-α2, phosphorylated AMPK-α2, PGC-1α, and PPAR-α in myocardial tissue. These findings suggest that GLP protects against ISO-induced myocardial ischemic injury by improving myocardial energy metabolism and reducing oxidative stress, with AMPK/PGC-1α/PPAR-α-related metabolic regulation potentially contributing to its cardioprotective effects.
ids: title:ganoderma lucidum polysaccharide protects against myocardial ischemic injury by restoring myocardial energy metabolism and alleviating oxidative stress in mice and ac16 cardiomyocytes

title: Perioperative management of SGLT2 inhibitors: balancing euglycaemic ketoacidosis risk and cardiorenal benefits.
abstract: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors are established therapies for type 2 diabetes, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease, creating a perioperative need to balance prevention of euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis (euDKA) against cardiorenal protection. Fasting, surgical stress, infection, reduced carbohydrate intake, insulin dose reduction, and hypovolaemia can amplify glycosuria and ketogenesis and precipitate euDKA. Most guidelines recommend withholding SGLT2 inhibitors for 3-4 days before elective surgery, although recommendations vary by agent, procedure, fasting duration, diabetes status, and monitoring capacity. Emerging evidence indicates competing perioperative risks and benefits. Inadequate withholding and emergency surgery are associated with high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and ketoacidosis, whereas observational studies associate preoperative use with lower risks of acute kidney injury and short-term mortality. Heart failure withdrawal studies further suggest that cardiovascular and volume-regulatory benefits may diminish rapidly after interruption. These findings challenge uniform withholding but do not support routine perioperative continuation. Management should be stratified by treatment indication, glycated haemoglobin, insulin dependence, hepatic and kidney function, infection and volume status, surgical urgency and invasiveness, expected fasting duration, and access to ketone and acid-base monitoring. Patients at high metabolic risk generally require an adequate preoperative withholding interval and intensified monitoring, whereas low-risk patients treated primarily for heart failure or chronic kidney disease require individualised multidisciplinary assessment. Future studies should define indication- and risk-based withholding and restart strategies and jointly evaluate euDKA, acute kidney injury, worsening heart failure, myocardial injury, mortality, and postoperative recovery.
ids: title:perioperative management of sglt2 inhibitors balancing euglycaemic ketoacidosis risk and cardiorenal benefits

title: Associations between CT-Based Body Composition and Cardiotoxicity and Overall Survival in Patients with Prostate Cancer.
abstract: The purpose of this study was to investigate the associations of parameters of computed tomography (CT)-based body composition with cancer treatment-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD) and with overall survival (OS) in patients with prostate cancer who received androgen deprivation therapy (ADT). Patients with prostate cancer treated with ADT were retrospectively included. Parameters of CT-based body composition, including the area and density of subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT), visceral adipose tissue (VAT) and skeletal muscle (SM), were measured on axial images at the third lumbar vertebra. The associations between body composition and CTRCD were assessed by logistic regression analysis. The associations between body composition and OS were assessed using Cox regression analysis. Among the 530 patients enrolled, 45 developed CTRCD, and 198 died during a median follow-up of 45 months (interquartile range, 23-54 months). Patients with CTRCD had a significantly lower SM index than patients without CTRCD (29.16 ± 3.66 vs. 38.3 ± 3.83 cm2/m2, respectively, P < 0.001). A lower SM index was associated with a significantly increased risk of CTRCD (odds ratio = 1.965, 95% CI: 1.459-3.472, P = 0.005) and a poor OS (hazard ratio = 2.201, 95% CI: 1.817-2.766, P = 0.008). Utilization of the CT-based SM index contributes to the baseline risk stratification of cardiotoxicity and OS in patients with prostate cancer treated with ADT.
ids: title:associations between ct based body composition and cardiotoxicity and overall survival in patients with prostate cancer

title: A hypothalamic neuronal population coordinates metabolic adaptations to cold.
abstract: Cold exposure increases feeding, thermogenesis, and energy expenditure to maintain body temperature and energy balance, but the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we identify cold-responsive neurons in the dorsal posterior periventricular hypothalamus that coordinate these adaptations. Activation of GABAergic or cold-activated neurons increased food intake, body temperature, and brown adipose tissue thermogenesis, whereas their inhibition attenuated cold-induced hyperphagia and thermogenesis. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing identified Lef1 as a marker of cold-activated neurons in this region. Activation of Lef1+ neurons recapitulated key cold responses, whereas silencing attenuated them. Lef1 positively regulated Kcnk2, which encodes the cold-sensitive potassium channel TREK-1. Cold reduced Kcnk2 expression and potassium currents, while pharmacological or genetic Kcnk2 inhibition increased feeding and body temperature. Conversely, Kcnk2 gain-of-function blunted cold responses. Together, these findings identify Lef1+ hypothalamic neurons and Kcnk2 modulation as a mechanism linking environmental temperature to neuronal activity and systemic metabolic adaptation.
ids: title:a hypothalamic neuronal population coordinates metabolic adaptations to cold

title: Dopamine receptor D1 is altered in atrial fibrillation-associated tissues and modulates Ang II-induced cardiomyocyte stress partly through PI3K/Akt signaling.
abstract: Background Atrial fibrillation (AF) is associated with atrial remodeling, oxidative stress, and inflammation; however, the molecular mechanisms underlying these processes remain unclear. We investigated whether dopamine receptor D1 (DRD1) is associated with AF-related cardiac phenotypes and whether DRD1 modulates cardiomyocyte responses to angiotensin II (Ang II)-induced stress. Methods DRD1 expression was examined in the GSE135445 epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) dataset and independently in the GSE41177 myocardial transcriptomic dataset of patients with AF and sinus rhythm. DRD1 expression and AF-associated phenotypes were assessed in C57BL/6 mice subjected to chronic Ang II infusion. In HL-1 cardiomyocytes, DRD1 was overexpressed before Ang II exposure, and the contribution of PI3K/Akt signaling was evaluated using LY294002. Results DRD1 expression was altered in EAT and downregulated in the myocardial tissue of patients with AF compared to sinus rhythm control. DRD1 expression was also reduced in the atrial tissue of Ang II-treated mice, which exhibited increased AF inducibility and duration. In HL-1 cardiomyocytes, Ang II reduced DRD1 expression, whereas DRD1 overexpression increased PI3K/Akt phosphorylation and attenuated Ang II-induced reductions in cell viability, LDH release, hypertrophic responses, ROS generation, oxidative stress, and NLRP3 inflammasome-associated signaling. LY294002 partially attenuated these effects. Conclusions DRD1 expression is altered in EAT and downregulated in the myocardial tissue of patients with AF and in experimental atrial remodeling. DRD1 overexpression protects cardiomyocytes against Ang II-induced stress, with PI3K/Akt signaling contributing to this effect. However, whether DRD1 causally regulates AF susceptibility in vivo remains to be established.
ids: title:dopamine receptor d1 is altered in atrial fibrillation associated tissues and modulates ang ii induced cardiomyocyte stress partly through pi3k akt signaling

title: Myocardial infarction treatment with a composite hydrogel containing metformin-induced vesicles of adipose-derived stem cells.
abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) leads to irreversible cardiomyocyte loss and adverse remodeling. Mesenchymal stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) have shown promise in cardiac repair, but their clinical translation has been strictly limited by the short retention time and rapid clearance phenomena at the injury site. Metformin preconditioning of adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs) is an effective way to enhance the yield of the EVs (Met-EVs). In this study, we incorporated Met-EVs into a composite hydrogel composed of decellularized extracellular matrices (dECMs) derived from porcine cardiac muscle and aortic adventitia, enabling sustained EV release and attenuation of inflammation after MI. In a rat MI model, the Met-EVs-laden dECM hydrogel (Met-EVs-dECM) significantly improved cardiac function recovery by enhancing cardiomyocyte survival, reducing cardiac apoptosis, and promoting angiogenesis. C1q/tumor necrosis factor-related protein 1 was identified as a contributor to the biological effects of Met-EVs, at least in part through the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway. Collectively, these findings demonstrate the therapeutic potential of the Met-EV-loaded dECM hydrogel for myocardial repair after MI.
ids: title:myocardial infarction treatment with a composite hydrogel containing metformin induced vesicles of adipose derived stem cells

title: Cold water exposure therapy and effects on insulin: a scoping review.
abstract: Context Cold water exposure (CWE) is a growing trend among health and wellness communities due to its effects on brown adipose tissue (BAT) activation and neurotransmitter modulation. However, its impact on insulin sensitivity and glucose metabolism in humans remains underexplored. Objectives This scoping review aims to evaluate the existing literature on the effects of CWE on insulin-related metabolic markers in humans and to identify the knowledge gaps that currently exist in this field of study. Methods A scoping review was conducted by two authors (JG and BM) according to the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) guidelines and framework. A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane databases was conducted on July 11, 2025, utilizing search strings developed by a trained librarian. Title and abstract screening, as well as full-text review and data extraction, were performed in a masked, duplicative fashion. Inclusion criteria required human studies published in English from 2000 onward that utilized CWE and measured insulin, glucose, or related metabolic outcomes. Results A total of 941 articles were identified, with 67 articles selected for further review. Ultimately, six studies met our inclusion criteria. These studies varied in participant demographics (male, female, mixed cohorts) and age groups ranging from 18 to 55+. The intervention duration included mostly acute sessions. The majority of studies (n=4) reported an improvement in insulin sensitivity and glucose utilization by peripheral tissues, as well as BAT utilization. However, the study by Sellers suggested increased insulin resistance, and the study by Hanssen et al. showed a decrease in cold-stimulated BAT glucose uptake. Only two studies utilized full-body CWE, whereas the remainder utilized cold suits or partial immersion techniques. Conclusions Current research suggests that non-shivering-inducing CWE can enhance insulin sensitivity and glucose metabolism in healthy humans. Extrapolating these findings to suggest application as an adjunct therapy for insulin resistance is premature. However, methodological variability and a lack of high-quality, long-duration studies highlight the need for further research, particularly distinguishing between cold suits and full-body-immersion protocols, to clarify their efficacy and clinical applicability.
ids: title:cold water exposure therapy and effects on insulin a scoping review

title: Normal weight obesity: a South Asian phenotype.
journal: Current opinion in endocrinology, diabetes, and obesity
abstract: Purpose of review Recent guidelines emphasize the significance of measuring adiposity rather than relying solely on BMI. This shift underscores the importance of normal-weight obesity (NWO), which is identified by assessing body fat percentage. This review presents recent advances in understanding NWO, including several substantial cohort studies that examine its prevalence, pathophysiology, and clinical implications. Recent findings The prevalence of NWO is notably high. Extensive cohort studies have established its association with increased cardiometabolic mortality, changes in microbiota diversity and composition, and alterations in body composition, including a reduction in brown adipose tissue. Body composition metrics, such as the android-gynoid ratio, have emerged as significant indicators of metabolic health. Additionally, the association with ultra-processed foods underscores the need to integrate nutrition and exercise regimens into treatment protocols. Summary NWO represents a clinically significant condition that requires early diagnosis to improve cardiometabolic outcomes.
ids: title:normal weight obesity a south asian phenotype

title: Association of Epicardial Adipose Tissue Thickness With Heart Rate Variability and Electrocardiographic Markers of Electrical Heterogeneity in Obesity.
journal: Annals of noninvasive electrocardiology : the official journal of the International Society for Holter and Noninvasive Electrocardiology, Inc
abstract: Obesity is associated with atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, but the links among excess adiposity, autonomic dysfunction, and electrical heterogeneity remain incompletely defined. We examined whether epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) thickness was associated with heart rate variability (HRV) indices and electrocardiographic markers of electrical heterogeneity in adults with obesity. In this cross-sectional study conducted between January 2023 and June 2025, 129 adults with obesity (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2) and 156 normal-weight controls (BMI < 25 kg/m2) with broadly similar group-level age and sex distributions were evaluated. EAT thickness was measured by transthoracic echocardiography. Autonomic modulation was assessed by 24-h HRV. Electrocardiograms were analyzed for P-wave dispersion (PWD), Tpeak-to-Tend (Tp-e) interval, Tp-e dispersion, and Tp-e/QT ratio. The prespecified primary endpoints were PWD and Tp-e interval. Compared with controls, individuals with obesity had greater EAT thickness (7.2 ± 1.1 vs. 4.2 ± 2.1 mm), higher PWD (30.9 ± 5.8 vs. 17.5 ± 2.4 ms), and longer Tp-e interval (96.2 ± 8.8 vs. 83.5 ± 7.4 ms; all p < 0.001). Between-group differences were 13.6 ms for PWD (95% CI 12.5-14.7) and 12.7 ms for Tp-e (95% CI 10.8-14.6). Obesity was also associated with lower SDNN and RMSSD, higher LF/HF ratio, and higher Tp-e dispersion, whereas Tp-e/QT showed only a nominal exploratory difference. In multivariable linear regression, EAT thickness remained independently associated with PWD (standardized β = 0.38, p < 0.001) and Tp-e interval (standardized β = 0.35, p < 0.001). Greater EAT thickness in obesity was associated with an unfavorable HRV profile and increased atrial and ventricular electrical heterogeneity. These findings are associative and should not be interpreted as clinical rhythm-risk stratification.
ids: title:association of epicardial adipose tissue thickness with heart rate variability and electrocardiographic markers of electrical heterogeneity in obesity

title: The Hidden Cost of Blue Light: Multiorgan Pathology Induced by LED Exposure in Mice
abstract: ABSTRACT Life evolved under broad-spectrum sunlight (300–3500 nm), but most modern light-emitting diodes (LEDs) emit within a restricted visible range (350-650 nm) leaving lighting environments that are short-wavelength dominant. We ask if chronic 450nm exposure dominant in LEDs alters metabolism and organ integrity in ageing mice environmentally exposed at 13 mW/cm² for 5 h/day over 40 weeks, at an intensity within the range of human environmental exposures. Mice exhibited progressive weight gain despite reduced food intake, with altered glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity over time. White adipose tissue mass increased, while brown adipose tissue weight and UCP1 protein levels remained unchanged. Relative organ weights (heart, liver, kidney, testis) were each reduced by ∼10%, with histopathology revealing fat deposition, hepatocellular degeneration, renal tubular damage, steatosis, and impaired testicular architecture. These findings demonstrate that chronic 450 nm light exposure is associated with metabolic alterations and multiorgan pathology in mice.
ids: title:the hidden cost of blue light multiorgan pathology induced by led exposure in mice

title: Obesity and Osteoporotic Fractures: Solving the Paradox.
journal: Indian journal of endocrinology and metabolism
abstract: Obesity is a global health issue linked to conditions like metabolic syndrome and heart disease, but its relationship with fracture risk is complex. While higher body mass index (BMI) is associated with increased bone mineral density (BMD) due to mechanical loading, it does not uniformly protect against fractures. Obese individuals face higher risks of proximal humerus and ankle fractures, along with propensity for increased falls and sarcopenic obesity. Higher fat mass, particularly visceral adiposity, correlates with lower bone quality and increased fracture risk, independent of BMD. Obesity triggers inflammatory pathways (e.g., TNF-α, Monocyte Chemotactic Protein-1 [MCP-1]) and adipokine imbalances (e.g., adiponectin, leptin), impairing bone formation and resorption. Vitamin D deficiency and secondary hyperparathyroidism further exacerbate cortical bone loss. Diagnostic challenges arise as dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry and FRAX tools may underestimate fracture risk in obesity. Preventive strategies emphasize lifestyle interventions, including moderate weight loss targeting subcutaneous fat, resistance training, and optimal dairy intake to enhance BMD.
ids: title:obesity and osteoporotic fractures solving the paradox
